sources.title: Tzolkʼin
sources.notes: The 20 day names and their meanings (after Miller and Taube 1993 and Wright 1989), and the good/bad days and their uses in three highland Guatemalan calendars, based on an 1854 manuscript by Vicente Hernández Spina as given by Weeks, Sachse and Prager (2009).

sources.title: Maya Daykeeping: Three Calendars from Highland Guatemala
sources.notes: Transcribes three divinatory calendars from highland Guatemala (including one of 1772) and Hernández Spina's 1854 notes on the days. Cited here through the Wikipedia summary; not read directly.
sources.author: John M. Weeks, Frauke Sachse and Christian M. Prager (eds.)

sources.title: Mesoamerican Long Count calendar
sources.notes: The GMT correlation (584,283): 13.0.0.0.0 4 Ajaw 8 Kumkʼu; the current bʼakʼtun began on 21 December 2012. Highland communities that still keep the 260-day count are consistent with it (Tedlock 1992).

sources.title: Haabʼ
sources.notes: The 365-day year of eighteen 20-day months plus the five Wayebʼ days, thought to be a dangerous time.

sources.title: Akan calendar
sources.notes: The six-day week (nnanson) and its day meanings, the seven-day week (nnawɔtwe) and its meanings, the 42-day adaduanan grid recorded in Kwahu and Bono, and the four dabɔne (Fɔdwo, Awukudae, Fofie, Akwasidae) with their rules. Mainly after Bartle (1978).

sources.title: Forty Days: The Akan Calendar
sources.publisher: Africa: Journal of the International African Institute 48(1), 80–84
sources.notes: The 42-day cycle and its special days; dates the dabɔne of 1978 (Akwasidae 8 Jan, Fodwo 23 Jan, Awukudae 1 Feb, Fofi 10 Feb). Cited through the Wikipedia article.
sources.author: Philip F. W. Bartle

sources.title: Akan name
sources.notes: Day names given to children by the day of the week they were born, with the meaning associated with each day.

sources.title: Igbo calendar
sources.notes: The four market days Eke, Orie, Afọ, Nkwọ; their link to the four directions (Isichei 1997); naming after the market day; the Nri year-counting festival Ịgụ Arọ "initially slated" for 18 February 2012, "an Nkwọ day".

sources.title: 建除十二神 (The twelve day officers)
sources.notes: Chinese Wikipedia. Quotes the Huainanzi (2nd century BCE), the Qin Day Books (Shuihudi), a Dunhuang almanac of 924 CE with one prohibition per officer, the Song official calendar, and the Qing rule (Xieji bianfang shu, 1741) used by almanacs today.

sources.title: Huainanzi, chapter 3: Tianwen xun (Treatise on the Patterns of Heaven)
sources.notes: "寅為建，卯為除，辰為滿，巳為平，主生。午為定，未為執，主陷。申為破，主衡。酉為危，主杓。戌為成，主少德。亥為收，主大德。子為開，主太歲。丑為閉，主太陰。"
sources.author: Liu An (ed.)

sources.title: Sexagenary cycle
sources.notes: Day counting by the sixty stem-branch pairs since the Shang oracle bones; the solar-term months (jiéyuè) and their branches; worked example: 1 October 1949 was a jiazi (甲子) day.

sources.title: Tithi
sources.notes: A tithi is the time for the Moon to gain 12° on the Sun; 30 to a lunar month; the tithi at sunrise is the tithi of the day; auspicious and inauspicious tithis.

sources.title: Paksha
sources.notes: The bright fortnight (Śukla Pakṣa, waxing, "considered auspicious") and the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇa Pakṣa, waning); amānta and pūrṇimānta month reckoning.

sources.title: Ekadashi
sources.notes: The 11th tithi of each fortnight: fasting for Vishnu; the three-day observance (one meal on Daśamī, fast on Ekādaśī, break the fast after sunrise on Dvādaśī) and lighter forms of the fast.

sources.title: Amavasya
sources.notes: The new-Moon tithi: fasting, and especially rites for the ancestors (śrāddha, tarpaṇa).

sources.title: Purnima
sources.notes: The full-Moon tithi; many festivals fall on the Pūrṇimā of particular months.

sources.title: Pradosha
sources.notes: Twice a month, on the 13th tithi: Shiva worship at twilight, with a fast (pradoṣa vrata).

sources.title: Sankashti Chaturthi
sources.notes: Each month on the 4th tithi of the dark fortnight: a fast for Ganesha, broken at night after seeing the Moon.

sources.title: Pratipada, Dvitiya, Tritiya, Chaturthi, Shashthi, Saptami, Ashtami, Navami, Dashami, Dvadashi, Chaturdashi (articles)
sources.notes: The Wikipedia articles on the individual tithis: what each is, and which yearly festivals fall on it in particular months.

cultures.name: Maya
cultures.people: Maya peoples; Kʼicheʼ, Ixil, Mam and other highland communities still keep the 260-day count
cultures.overview: The 260-day tzolkʼin (20 day names with 13 numbers) runs alongside the 365-day haabʼ. Daykeepers (Aj Kʼij) in highland Guatemala still use it to choose days for actions.

cultures.name: Chinese
cultures.people: Han Chinese and the Chinese diaspora; printed almanacs are still sold every year
cultures.overview: Days are counted in a cycle of sixty stem-branch pairs, and almanacs name what is suitable and unsuitable each day. One of the oldest layers is the twelve day officers (建除), found in Qin Day Books of the 3rd century BCE.

cultures.name: Vedic Hindu
cultures.people: Hindus in South Asia and worldwide
cultures.overview: The Hindu almanac (pañcāṅga) counts lunar days called tithis: thirty to a lunar month, fifteen in the bright half and fifteen in the dark half. Fasts and festivals are kept on particular tithis.

systems.name: Tzolkʼin (260-day count)
systems.day_rule: Twenty named days run in order alongside the numbers 1 to 13; the same name and number meet again after 260 days.
systems.description: The 260-day count. Each of the twenty day names has its own character; daykeepers use it to choose good days for actions.
systems.uncertainty: The day meanings here come from one 19th-century highland source (Hernández Spina, 1854) and from modern scholarly summaries; daykeepers in different towns read the days differently.

systems.name: Haabʼ (365-day year)
systems.day_rule: Eighteen months of twenty days, then five extra days (Wayebʼ); no leap day, so it slowly drifts against the seasons.
systems.description: The 365-day vague year that runs alongside the tzolkʼin.

systems.name: Six-day week
systems.translation: "Seven days" (counting the first and last day both)
systems.day_rule: Six named days in a row (Fo, Nwuna, Nkyi, Kuru, Kwa, Mono). Running beside the seven-day week, it makes the 42-day adaduanan.
systems.description: The older Akan six-day week. Its days carry meanings of judgement, funerals, taboo, the town, freedom and fresh starts.
systems.uncertainty: Recorded in Kwahu and Bono (Bartle 1978, Rattray); other Akan states may differ. Dates are counted from the published Akwasidae dates of 2026, which agree with Bartle's 1978 dates.

systems.name: Seven-day week
systems.translation: "Eight days" (counting the first and last day both)
systems.day_rule: The same seven days as the Gregorian week, each with an Akan name and meaning. Children are named after the day they were born.
systems.description: The Akan seven-day week. Each day has a meaning and gives a day name to everyone born on it (Kofi for Friday, Ama for Saturday…).

systems.name: The twelve day officers
systems.day_rule: Each day is ruled by one of twelve 'officers', Jian (建) to Bi (閉), in turn. The day whose earthly branch matches the month's branch is Jian; the solar-term months begin at the twelve 'jie' terms (Lichun, Jingzhe…), and on the day a new month begins the officer repeats.
systems.description: One of the oldest day-choosing systems in Chinese almanacs: in the Qin Day Books (3rd century BCE), the Huainanzi (2nd century BCE), and every Tongshu (almanac) printed today.
systems.uncertainty: Almanacs differ on which items each officer allows or forbids; this record gives the Huainanzi's grouping, the Dunhuang almanac of 924 CE, and the Song and Qing rules as quoted by Chinese Wikipedia.

systems.name: Tithi (lunar day)
systems.day_rule: A tithi is the time the Moon takes to gain 12° on the Sun (about 19 to 27 hours). The tithi in force at sunrise is the tithi of the day, so a tithi is sometimes skipped or repeated.
systems.month_rule: Thirty tithis to a lunar month: Śukla (bright) Pratipadā to Pūrṇimā (full Moon), then Kṛṣṇa (dark) Pratipadā to Amāvasyā (new Moon). In the amānta reckoning (south India) the month ends at Amāvasyā; in the pūrṇimānta (north India) at Pūrṇimā.
systems.description: The lunar day of the Hindu pañcāṅga, one of its five parts with the weekday, nakṣatra, yoga and karaṇa.
systems.uncertainty: Tithi times depend on place (sunrise) and on the method (traditional Sūrya Siddhānta reckoning or modern ephemerides); almanacs for different cities can differ by a day at a boundary.

cycles.name: Twenty day names
cycles.description: The twenty day names of the tzolkʼin, from Imix to Ajaw.
cycles.anchor_note: 21 December 2012 was 13.0.0.0.0, 4 Ajaw in the GMT correlation (584,283). The highland Guatemalan count that daykeepers still keep agrees with this correlation.
cycles.regional_note: Highland daykeepers begin and read the day in their own way; one 19th-century source is quoted here.

cycles.name: Haabʼ year
cycles.description: The 365 days of the haabʼ, counted from 0 Pop; positions 360 to 364 are the five Wayebʼ days.
cycles.anchor_note: 21 December 2012 was 3 Kʼankʼin (GMT correlation): month 14 (Kʼankʼin) day 3, so position 13 × 20 + 3 = 263.

cycles.name: Six-day week
cycles.description: Fo, Nwuna, Nkyi, Kuru, Kwa, Mono.
cycles.anchor_note: Akwasidae is Kuru-Kwasi (Kuru of the six-day week on a Sunday) in the 42-day grid; Akwasidae fell on 1 February 2026 in the published listing. Bartle's 1978 dates count to the same days.

cycles.name: Seven-day week
cycles.anchor_note: The Akan and English seven-day weeks are the same: Kwasiada is Sunday. 1 February 2026 was a Sunday.

cycles.name: Market week
cycles.description: Eke, Orie, Afọ, Nkwọ: four market days that repeat without a break.
cycles.anchor_note: The Nri year-counting festival Ịgụ Arọ was initially slated for 18 February 2012, "an Nkwọ day". That fixes the Nri count; other towns' market days can fall on a different day of the cycle.
cycles.regional_note: This is the count of the Nri area. The order Eke, Orie, Afọ, Nkwọ is the same everywhere, but which day is Eke differs between communities; check your own town's market.

sources.quote: 18 February (an Nkwọ day on the third week of February)

cycles.name: Twelve day officers
cycles.description: 建 Jian, 除 Chu, 滿 Man, 平 Ping, 定 Ding, 執 Zhi, 破 Po, 危 Wei, 成 Cheng, 收 Shou, 開 Kai, 閉 Bi. Dated by rule, not by a plain 12-day count: see the day rule.
cycles.anchor_note: No single anchor: the officer is worked out from the day's stem-branch (1 October 1949 was 甲子) and the Sun's position (the solar-term month).

cycle_positions.name: Wayebʼ, day 1 of 5
cycle_positions.meaning: The five nameless days at the end of the 365-day year were thought a dangerous time: "portals between the mortal realm and the Underworld dissolved" (Foster 2002). People kept customs to ward off evil spirits; they would not leave their homes or wash their hair.
cycle_positions.uncertainty: Customs described for the ancient Maya in a modern summary; the haabʼ drifts against the seasons (no leap day).

cycle_positions.name: Fo
cycle_positions.meaning: Judgement day: "guilty verdict (passing sentence)"; also called Bemim, "not guilty verdict".
cycle_positions.uncertainty: Recorded in Kwahu and Bono (Bartle 1978, Rattray); other Akan states may differ. Dates are counted from the published Akwasidae dates of 2026, which agree with Bartle's 1978 dates.

cycle_positions.name: Nwuna
cycle_positions.meaning: Sleep (death) day; funerals day; covered day.
cycle_positions.uncertainty: Recorded in Kwahu and Bono (Bartle 1978, Rattray); other Akan states may differ. Dates are counted from the published Akwasidae dates of 2026, which agree with Bartle's 1978 dates.

cycle_positions.uncertainty: Recorded in Kwahu and Bono (Bartle 1978, Rattray); other Akan states may differ. Dates are counted from the published Akwasidae dates of 2026, which agree with Bartle's 1978 dates.

cycle_positions.name: Kwasiada
cycle_positions.meaning: Under day (awiase, 'under the sun'): the universe, everything. Day names for people born on it: Kwasi, Akosua.

cycle_positions.name: Ɛdwoada
cycle_positions.meaning: Quiet (peace) day; calm. Day names for people born on it: Kwadwo, Adwoa.

cycle_positions.name: Ɛbenada
cycle_positions.meaning: Birthday of the ocean; heat, boiling, cooking. Day names for people born on it: Kwabena, Abena.

cycle_positions.name: Wukuada
cycle_positions.meaning: Birthday of Spider (Ananse). Day names for people born on it: Kwaku, Akua.

cycle_positions.name: Yawoada
cycle_positions.meaning: Birthday of the Earth (a woman); power. The Asante say Asase Yaa, the Earth, was created on a Thursday. Day names for people born on it: Yaw, Yaa.

cycle_positions.name: Efiada
cycle_positions.meaning: Fertility (in some Fante states, the Earth's birthday). Day names for people born on it: Kofi, Afua.

cycle_positions.name: Memeneda
cycle_positions.meaning: Birthday of the Supreme or Sky God (a man); respected, ancient. Day names for people born on it: Kwame, Ama.

cycle_positions.name: Fɔdwo
cycle_positions.meaning: Fo of the six-day week on a Monday. With Fofie, one of the two dabɔne for the tutelary spirits (abosom): purification and the spirits of rivers and caves.
cycle_positions.uncertainty: Recorded in Kwahu and Bono (Bartle 1978, Rattray); other Akan states may differ. Dates are counted from the published Akwasidae dates of 2026, which agree with Bartle's 1978 dates.

cycle_positions.name: Awukudae
cycle_positions.meaning: Kuru of the six-day week on a Wednesday: the Wednesday Adae (Wukuo-Adae). Libations and food are offered to the blackened stools of the ancestors.
cycle_positions.uncertainty: Recorded in Kwahu and Bono (Bartle 1978, Rattray); other Akan states may differ. Dates are counted from the published Akwasidae dates of 2026, which agree with Bartle's 1978 dates.

cycle_positions.name: Fofie
cycle_positions.meaning: Fo of the six-day week on a Friday. With Fɔdwo, a dabɔne for the tutelary spirits: purification and the spirits of rivers and caves.
cycle_positions.uncertainty: Recorded in Kwahu and Bono (Bartle 1978, Rattray); other Akan states may differ. Dates are counted from the published Akwasidae dates of 2026, which agree with Bartle's 1978 dates.

lunar_days.name: Śukla Pratipadā
lunar_days.meaning: The first tithi of the Śukla (bright, waxing) fortnight. The bright fortnight is "considered auspicious". Yearly festivals on this tithi in particular months: Gudi Padwa and Ugadi (new year, Chaitra); Govardhan Puja and Bali Pratipada (Kartika).
lunar_days.uncertainty: Calculated: the tithi at sunrise in Ujjain (the traditional meridian of Indian astronomy). Almanacs for your own city can differ by a day where a tithi begins or ends near sunrise.

lunar_days.uncertainty: Calculated: the tithi at sunrise in Ujjain (the traditional meridian of Indian astronomy). Almanacs for your own city can differ by a day where a tithi begins or ends near sunrise.

meanings.subject: cycle_position
meanings.meaning: Eke is the market day of the east: the four days correspond to the four cardinal points. Each community holds a market named after one of the days, and children were once named after their market day (e.g. Okeke, Mgbeke).
meanings.uncertainty: The days' directions are from Isichei (1997) as cited by Wikipedia. Names like these are now used less often.

recommendations.historical_practice: Imox is a bad day, associated with the insane, on which the priests of the sun pray that harm may come to their enemies through evil spirits.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Iq is a bad day, symbolic of the destructive forces of nature; that power is localized in stone idols, who are honored with incense, roses, candles, pine needles and aguardiente. Tumours and painful swellings are attributed to the influence of this day.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Aqabal is a bad day, on which the priests of the sun go to shrines to pray against their enemies. The day is symbolic of evil in general and of slanderers in particular. (A modern summary adds that a low-numbered Akʼbʼal is a good day for a wedding.)
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Kat is a bad day in the same sense as Aqabal, symbolic of evil in general. (A modern summary says Kʼan is a good day for building or maintaining a house.)
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Kan is a bad day. It brings sickness and is symbolic of the arbitrary cruelty of nature.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Kame is recorded as a bad day by one 19th-century source and as a good day by a 20th-century one (Ruth Bunzel). It is symbolic of the dissolution by death of everything good and evil, and a good day to confess one's wrongs and ask for pardon.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Keej is a good day on which wishes are made. It is a good day to ask favours and to commemorate ancestors.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Qanil is a good day, sacred to fertility gods, associated with human nourishment, the growth of crops, the cycle of death and rebirth, and the milpa (maize field). After the harvest is completed, thanksgiving is made on Qanil.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Toj is a bad day, symbolized by sickness, and anyone born on it will be perverse. It is a good day to wish sickness upon an enemy.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Tzi is a bad day, symbolized by sexual depravity. No ceremonies must ever be held on this day.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Batz is a bad day, symbolized by paralysis. According to some it is a good day, symbolic of the ancestors. Every 260 days, 8 Batz is the great initiation day of daykeepers in Momostenango and Santa Cruz del Quiché.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: E is a good day, symbolized by destiny, fortune and the essential characteristics of one's personality. It is a day on which marriages may be held, and sacrifices to benign deities may be made.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Aj is a good day, consecrated to fertility gods, herdsmen and domesticated animals. The day is symbolic of one's destiny as embodied in one's nagual (animal companion spirit). (A modern summary says a low-numbered Bʼen is a good day for a wedding.)
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Ix is a good day, sacred to the mountain and forest spirits. On this day protection may be sought from wolves and wild predators, in favour of flocks and animals. The day is symbolic of the creative force and of the earth itself.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Tzikin is the most excellent day of all. Double offerings are made at shrines, in forests and in caves. It is a day on which wishes may be made, forgiveness may be sought, and important matters may be finalized.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Ajmaq is also a very good day, one sacred to the spirits that preside over good health.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Noj is an auspicious day, on which good judgement may be prayed for. The day is symbolic of humanity's moral and amoral qualities.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Tijax is a good day. It is a day of verbal arguments, and a good day to confess sins.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Kawoq is recognised as an indifferent day or a bad day. It is symbolic of the malice of the dead.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: Ajpu is an indifferent day, neither a bad nor a good portent, on which the power of the ancestors is embodied by the house itself.
recommendations.uncertainty: From Hernández Spina's 1854 manuscript on three highland Guatemalan calendars, as summarised (via Weeks, Sachse and Prager 2009) by Wikipedia. Daykeepers in other towns and times read the days differently; the day's number (1 to 13) also changes its strength.

recommendations.historical_practice: During Wayebʼ people would not leave their homes, and would not wash their hair.
recommendations.modern_interpretation: Keep these five days quiet: stay close to home and leave big starts until the new year begins (modern suggestion).

recommendations.historical_practice: No farming may be carried out on any dabɔne, but work as such is not banned: hunting and gathering are usually permitted, and people may fetch firewood or food reaped the day before, so long as no weeding is done. Communal labour is often done on the dabɔne that are not filled with ritual.
recommendations.uncertainty: Recorded in Kwahu and Bono (Bartle 1978, Rattray); other Akan states may differ. Dates are counted from the published Akwasidae dates of 2026, which agree with Bartle's 1978 dates.

recommendations.historical_practice: Suitable on a Jian day: opening a market, drawing up contracts, trading, receiving money, setting out on a journey, raising the roof beam, building, breaking ground, treating illness, taking a teacher, meeting relatives and friends. Avoid: pulling down a house, digging the earth, funerals and burials, demolition, digging wells, going by boat.
recommendations.uncertainty: As listed in modern almanacs following the Qing rule (Chinese Wikipedia, 現代作法); our translation. Note it lists breaking ground under both columns in different almanacs.

recommendations.historical_practice: In the Song official calendar (會元曆), days of Jian, Ping, Po and Shou were "not used" each month (每月逢建、平、破、收，日皆不用) for choosing days.
recommendations.uncertainty: Quoted by Hong Mai (Rongzhai suibi) as given in Chinese Wikipedia.

recommendations.historical_practice: Ekādaśī: a fast for Vishnu, to gain control over the mind and senses. Strictly, no food or water from sunrise; many keep a lighter fast (only water, only milk, only fruit, or one meal).
recommendations.uncertainty: Calculated: the tithi at sunrise in Ujjain (the traditional meridian of Indian astronomy). Almanacs for your own city can differ by a day where a tithi begins or ends near sunrise.
recommendations.modern_interpretation: If you fast, keep it gentle and right for your health (modern suggestion).

recommendations.historical_practice: Amāvasyā is particularly associated with the ancestors (pitṛs): holy dips in rivers, special pūjās, śrāddha rites, tarpaṇa (water offerings) and piṇḍa (rice-ball) offerings. Many fast.
recommendations.uncertainty: Calculated: the tithi at sunrise in Ujjain (the traditional meridian of Indian astronomy). Almanacs for your own city can differ by a day where a tithi begins or ends near sunrise.
recommendations.modern_interpretation: A day to remember your ancestors: light a lamp, say their names, give food (modern suggestion).
